name: My Favorite Spacetimes
description: A catalogue of exact solutions of Einstein's field equations. For each spacetime: its name, a description, tags, signature and the conventions shared by its charts, and for each coordinate chart the coordinates, their domains, the parameters, the chart's own conventions, the line element, the nonzero metric components and the curvature invariants. Mathematics is LaTeX.
note: The catalogue page chooses a spacetime in the browser and has no address per spacetime, so page_url is the catalogue itself. data_url is the full record the page draws from: Christoffel symbols, Riemann, Ricci, Einstein and Weyl tensors, geodesic equations and the history with its references.

spacetimes.name: Aichelburg-Sexl Ultraboost
spacetimes.description: The gravitational field of a massless particle, the Schwarzschild field boosted to the speed of light with its energy held fixed. Spacetime is flat on either side of a single null plane, which carries an impulsive gravitational shock wave with the particle at its centre.
spacetimes.convention: We keep factors of $G$ and $c$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.

charts.name: Cartesian

parameters.description: Newton's gravitational constant
Energy of the massless source, the limit of $Mc^2/\sqrt{1 - V^2/c^2}$ as its rest mass $M$ goes to zero and its speed $V$ to $c$
An arbitrary length; changing it moves $v$ behind the shock by a constant, which is a change of coordinates

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $x$, $y$, and $z$ lengths, and $\delta$ is the Dirac delta, a prime on it a derivative with respect to its argument. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
charts.line_element: ds^2 = -c^2dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2 - \dfrac{4GE}{c^4}\ln\left(\dfrac{x^2 + y^2}{\rho_0^2}\right)\delta(ct - z)\left(c\,dt - dz\right)^2

charts.name: Null Cartesian

parameters.description: Newton's gravitational constant
Energy of the massless source, the limit of $Mc^2/\sqrt{1 - V^2/c^2}$ as its rest mass $M$ goes to zero and its speed $V$ to $c$
An arbitrary length; changing it moves $v$ behind the shock by a constant, which is a change of coordinates

charts.convention: We use the null coordinates $u = ct - z$ and $v = ct + z$, both lengths, with $x$ and $y$ the transverse lengths, and $\delta$ is the Dirac delta, a prime on it a derivative with respect to its argument. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

charts.name: Null Cylindrical

parameters.description: Newton's gravitational constant
Energy of the massless source, the limit of $Mc^2/\sqrt{1 - V^2/c^2}$ as its rest mass $M$ goes to zero and its speed $V$ to $c$
An arbitrary length; changing it moves $v$ behind the shock by a constant, which is a change of coordinates

charts.convention: We use the null coordinates $u = ct - z$ and $v = ct + z$, both lengths, with $\rho$ the distance from the axis of the source and $\phi$ the angle about it, and $\delta$ is the Dirac delta, a prime on it a derivative with respect to its argument. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

spacetimes.name: Alcubierre Warp Drive
spacetimes.description: A warp bubble metric that contracts space ahead of a ship and expands it behind, allowing travel that is effectively faster than light without locally exceeding light speed. It requires negative energy density (exotic matter) to sustain the bubble.

charts.name: Cartesian

parameters.description: Bubble velocity in units of $c$, an arbitrary function of $t$ alone. The centre of the bubble follows the world line $x = x_s(t)$ with $dx_s/dt = c\,v_s(t)$, and nothing in the solution bounds it, so $v_s > 1$ is allowed and is the whole point of the construction: the ship rides at rest in its own flat patch and no local measurement ever catches it outrunning a light ray. The prime is the derivative along the chart coordinate, $v_s' = dv_s/d(ct)$, so it carries an inverse length.

Shape function, dimensionless, an arbitrary function of the four coordinates. It is $1$ at the centre of the bubble and $0$ far outside it, and the wall is wherever it falls between, so every derivative of $f$ is supported on the wall alone and the spacetime is flat everywhere else. Alcubierre's own choice is the radial profile $f(r_s)$ built from hyperbolic tangents, with $r_s = \sqrt{(x - x_s(t))^2 + y^2 + z^2}$ the distance from the centre of the bubble, but no component needs it. A profile that depends on $t$ and $x$ only through $x - x_s(t)$ obeys $\partial_t f = -v_s\,\partial_x f$ in this chart, and that is the one relation the components are not allowed to assume, since they are identities for an arbitrary $f$.

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $x$, $y$, and $z$ lengths. The velocity $v_s$ of the bubble is in units of $c$, so its centre follows $x = x_s(t)$ with $dx_s/dt = c\,v_s$, and the shape function $f$ is a dimensionless function of all four coordinates. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, where $\partial_t = c^{-1}\partial/\partial t$ and $v_s' = dv_s/d(ct)$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
charts.ricci_scalar: R = 2 v_s\,\partial_t\partial_x f + 2 v_s'\,\partial_x f + 2 v_s^2\,\left(\partial_x f\right)^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}v_s^2\,\left(\partial_y f\right)^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}v_s^2\,\left(\partial_z f\right)^2 + 2 v_s^2\,f\,\partial_x^2 f
charts.kretschmann: K = 4\left(v_s\,\partial_t\partial_x f + v_s'\,\partial_x f + v_s^2\left(\partial_x f\right)^2 + v_s^2 f\,\partial_x^2 f\right)^2 + 2\left(v_s\,\partial_t\partial_y f + v_s'\,\partial_y f + v_s^2 f\,\partial_x\partial_y f + 2v_s^2\,\partial_x f\,\partial_y f\right)^2 + 2\left(v_s\,\partial_t\partial_z f + v_s'\,\partial_z f + v_s^2 f\,\partial_x\partial_z f + 2v_s^2\,\partial_x f\,\partial_z f\right)^2 - 2v_s^2\left(\left(\partial_y f\right)^2 + \left(\partial_z f\right)^2\right)\left(v_s\,\partial_t\partial_x f + v_s'\,\partial_x f + v_s^2\left(\partial_x f\right)^2 + v_s^2 f\,\partial_x^2 f\right) + \dfrac{11}{4}v_s^4\left(\left(\partial_y f\right)^2 + \left(\partial_z f\right)^2\right)^2 - 2v_s^2\left(\left(\partial_x\partial_y f\right)^2 + \left(\partial_x\partial_z f\right)^2 + \left(\partial_y^2 f\right)^2 + \left(\partial_z^2 f\right)^2 + 2\left(\partial_y\partial_z f\right)^2\right)

spacetimes.name: Anti-de Sitter
spacetimes.description: The maximally symmetric vacuum solution with constant negative curvature, arising from a negative cosmological constant. Its conformal boundary underpins the AdS/CFT correspondence in theoretical physics.

charts.name: Static global

parameters.description: Anti-de Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = -3/L^2$; every sectional curvature of this spacetime is $-1/L^2$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Poincare patch

parameters.description: Anti-de Sitter radius, the same length as in the global chart, with $\Lambda = -3/L^2$; the conformal boundary where the dual field theory lives is $z \to 0$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $x$, $y$, and $z$ lengths. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

spacetimes.name: Black Hole Threaded by a Cosmic String
spacetimes.description: A Schwarzschild black hole with a straight cosmic string through it. Off the axis it is Schwarzschild's vacuum, and around the whole axis, horizon included, a wedge is missing whose angle the string's tension sets, which lowers the horizon's area and the black hole's energy at a fixed mass.
spacetimes.convention: The Schwarzschild radius is $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, and $b = 1 - 4G\mu/c^2$ for a string of mass per unit length $\mu$, so the deficit angle is $2\pi(1 - b) = 8\pi G\mu/c^2$. We keep factors of $c$ explicit.

charts.name: Static

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, with $M$ the gravitational mass
$b = 1 - 4G\mu/c^2$, with $\mu$ the string's mass per unit length, equal to its tension, $0 < b \le 1$; the deficit angle is $2\pi(1 - b)$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\phi$ periodic in $2\pi$, the deficit carried by $g_{\phi\phi} = b^2r^2\sin^2\theta$.

charts.name: Static with the Wedge Removed

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, with $M$ the gravitational mass
$b = 1 - 4G\mu/c^2$, with $\mu$ the string's mass per unit length, equal to its tension, $0 < b \le 1$; the deficit angle is $2\pi(1 - b)$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \tilde\phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\tilde\phi = b\phi$ periodic in $2\pi b$, so that the line element is Schwarzschild's.

charts.name: Outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, with $M$ the gravitational mass
$b = 1 - 4G\mu/c^2$, with $\mu$ the string's mass per unit length, equal to its tension, $0 < b \le 1$; the deficit angle is $2\pi(1 - b)$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the retarded time $u = ct - r - r_s\ln\left|r/r_s - 1\right|$ a length and $\phi$ periodic in $2\pi$.

charts.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, with $M$ the gravitational mass
$b = 1 - 4G\mu/c^2$, with $\mu$ the string's mass per unit length, equal to its tension, $0 < b \le 1$; the deficit angle is $2\pi(1 - b)$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the advanced time $v = ct + r + r_s\ln\left|r/r_s - 1\right|$ a length and $\phi$ periodic in $2\pi$.

spacetimes.name: Bañados-Teitelboim-Zanelli Black Hole
spacetimes.description: A rotating black hole in three spacetime dimensions with a negative cosmological constant. It has constant negative curvature everywhere, being anti-de Sitter space with points identified by a discrete boost, and it carries a temperature and an entropy that can be computed exactly.
spacetimes.convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, with $M = 8Gm/c^2$ and $J = 8Gj/c^3$ for a hole of mass $m$ and angular momentum $j$, and $G$ Newton's constant in three dimensions. We write $N^2 = r^2/\ell^2 - M + J^2/(4r^2)$, which vanishes on the horizons $r_\pm^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}M\ell^2\left(1 \pm \sqrt{1 - J^2/(M^2\ell^2)}\right)$.

charts.name: Stationary

parameters.description: Anti-de Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = -1/\ell^2$
Mass, dimensionless, $M = 8Gm/c^2$ for a hole of mass $m$, with $G$ Newton's constant in three dimensions
Angular momentum, a length, $J = 8Gj/c^3$ for a hole of angular momentum $j$; a horizon exists only for $|J| \le M\ell$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Anti-de Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = -1/\ell^2$
Mass, dimensionless, $M = 8Gm/c^2$ for a hole of mass $m$, with $G$ Newton's constant in three dimensions
Angular momentum, a length, $J = 8Gj/c^3$ for a hole of angular momentum $j$; a horizon exists only for $|J| \le M\ell$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \tilde\phi)$, with the advanced time $v$ a length, $dv = c\,dt + dr/N^2$ and $d\tilde\phi = d\phi + J\,dr/(2r^2N^2)$.

charts.name: Outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Anti-de Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = -1/\ell^2$
Mass, dimensionless, $M = 8Gm/c^2$ for a hole of mass $m$, with $G$ Newton's constant in three dimensions
Angular momentum, a length, $J = 8Gj/c^3$ for a hole of angular momentum $j$; a horizon exists only for $|J| \le M\ell$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \tilde\phi)$, with the retarded time $u$ a length, $du = c\,dt - dr/N^2$ and $d\tilde\phi = d\phi - J\,dr/(2r^2N^2)$.

spacetimes.name: Bertotti-Robinson Electrovacuum
spacetimes.description: A conformally flat electrovacuum solution with uniform electromagnetic field, geometrically the product of two spaces of two dimensions each (AdS₂ × S²). It appears as the limit near the horizon of an extremal Reissner-Nordström black hole.
spacetimes.convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit. The single parameter $b$ is the common radius of the two factors, and every sphere of the spacetime has the areal radius $b$. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.

charts.name: Static throat

parameters.description: Common radius of the two factors, a length; it is fixed by the field through $b^2 = \dfrac{c^4}{8\pi G u}$, where $u$ is the energy density of the uniform electromagnetic field, and it equals the charge radius $r_q$ of the extremal Reissner-Nordstrom hole whose throat this is

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ a time and $r$ a length along the AdS$_2$ factor. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Poincaré

parameters.description: Common radius of the two factors, a length; it is fixed by the field through $b^2 = \dfrac{c^4}{8\pi G u}$, where $u$ is the energy density of the uniform electromagnetic field, and it equals the charge radius $r_q$ of the extremal Reissner-Nordstrom hole whose throat this is

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ a time and $x$ a length along the AdS$_2$ factor, related to the static chart by $rx = b^2$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

spacetimes.name: Bianchi Anisotropic Cosmologies
spacetimes.description: A family of spatially homogeneous but generally anisotropic cosmologies classified by the symmetry group of their spatial slices. They generalize FLRW models to study anisotropy in the early universe.
spacetimes.convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.

charts.name: Type I, Cartesian

parameters.description: Scale factor along $x$ ($a_1 > 0$), dimensionless
Scale factor along $y$ ($a_2 > 0$), dimensionless
Scale factor along $z$ ($a_3 > 0$); the three are independent, and the model is isotropic only where they agree

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, with $t$ a cosmic time and $x$, $y$, and $z$ comoving Cartesian lengths, and the three scale factors $a_1(t)$, $a_2(t)$, and $a_3(t)$ are arbitrary, positive, and dimensionless. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a prime is the derivative with respect to that chart time, $a_i' = \dfrac{da_i}{d(ct)} = \dfrac{1}{c}\dfrac{da_i}{dt}$ and $a_i'' = \dfrac{1}{c^2}\dfrac{d^2a_i}{dt^2}$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

spacetimes.name: C-Metric Accelerating Black Holes
spacetimes.description: An exact vacuum solution describing two black holes that accelerate away from each other, driven by a cosmic string or a strut along their axis of symmetry. With the acceleration set to zero it is the Schwarzschild black hole.

charts.name: Spherical

parameters.description: Geometric mass, $m = GM/c^2$, which is a length; the black hole horizon sits at $r = 2m$
Acceleration, an inverse length, with $2\alpha m < 1$; the acceleration horizon sits at $r = 1/\alpha$
A pure number scaling the angle about the axis; $C = 1/(1 + 2\alpha m)$ makes the half axis $\theta = 0$ regular and leaves a cosmic string along $\theta = \pi$

charts.convention: We use the coordinates of Jerry Griffiths, Pavel Krtouš, and Jiří Podolský, $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Hong-Teo

parameters.description: Geometric mass, $m = GM/c^2$, which is a length; the black hole horizon sits at $y = 1/(2\alpha m)$
Acceleration, an inverse length, with $2\alpha m < 1$; the acceleration horizon sits at $y = 1$
A pure number scaling the angle about the axis; $C = 1/(1 + 2\alpha m)$ makes the half axis $x = 1$ regular and leaves a cosmic string along $x = -1$

charts.convention: We use the coordinates of Kenneth Hong and Edward Teo, $(\tau, y, x, \phi)$, all dimensionless and related to the spherical coordinates by $\tau = \alpha ct$, $y = 1/(\alpha r)$, and $x = \cos\theta$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
charts.line_element: ds^2 = \dfrac{1}{\alpha^2\left(x + y\right)^2}\left(\left(1 - y^2\right)\left(1 - 2\alpha m y\right)d\tau^2 - \dfrac{dy^2}{\left(1 - y^2\right)\left(1 - 2\alpha m y\right)} + \dfrac{dx^2}{\left(1 - x^2\right)\left(1 + 2\alpha m x\right)} + C^2\left(1 - x^2\right)\left(1 + 2\alpha m x\right)d\phi^2\right)

spacetimes.name: Curzon-Chazy Particle
spacetimes.description: A static, axially symmetric vacuum field whose Weyl potential is Newton's potential of a point mass, found by Jean Chazy in 1924 and H. E. J. Curzon in 1925. Its singularity is a naked ring of infinite circumference, and the curvature there depends on the direction of approach.
spacetimes.convention: The mass parameter $m = GM/c^2$ is a length. We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.

charts.name: Weyl

parameters.description: Mass parameter, a length, $m = GM/c^2$ with $M$ the mass at spatial infinity
Distance from the origin in the flat space of Weyl's coordinates; Weyl's two functions are $\psi = -m/R$ and $\gamma = -m^2\rho^2/(2R^4)$

charts.convention: We use Weyl's canonical coordinates $(t, \rho, \phi, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\rho$ and $z$ lengths, and write $R = \sqrt{\rho^2 + z^2}$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Spherical

parameters.description: Mass parameter, a length, $m = GM/c^2$ with $M$ the mass at spatial infinity

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ with $\rho = r\sin\theta$ and $z = r\cos\theta$, so that $r$ is Weyl's $R$, and with $t$ carrying dimensions of time. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

spacetimes.name: de Sitter
spacetimes.description: The maximally symmetric vacuum solution with constant positive curvature, driven by a positive cosmological constant. It models an exponentially expanding empty universe and describes both inflation and the far future of our cosmos.

charts.name: Static Spherical

parameters.description: Cosmological constant, $\Lambda > 0$, carrying an inverse length squared. The horizon sits at $r = \sqrt{3/\Lambda}$ and the expansion rate of the flat slicing is $H = c\sqrt{\Lambda/3}$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
charts.line_element: ds^2 = -\left(1 - \dfrac{\Lambda r^2}{3}\right)c^2 dt^2 + \dfrac{dr^2}{1 - \dfrac{\Lambda r^2}{3}} + r^2 d\Omega^2

charts.name: Flat Slicing

parameters.description: Hubble rate, $H = c\sqrt{\Lambda/3}$, so that $\dfrac{3H^2}{c^2} = \Lambda$ and the horizon radius of the static patch is $c/H$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $x$, $y$, and $z$ comoving lengths, and the Hubble rate $H$ in place of $\Lambda$, related by $3H^2/c^2 = \Lambda$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

spacetimes.name: Gibbons-Maeda-Garfinkle-Horowitz-Strominger Dilaton Black Hole
spacetimes.description: The static, spherically symmetric charged black hole of low energy string theory, a solution of Einstein's equations with a Maxwell field and a scalar field, the dilaton, coupled to it. On the plane of time and radius its metric is Schwarzschild's, with one horizon at the Schwarzschild radius for every charge and no inner horizon, and the area of its spheres vanishes at the singularity.
spacetimes.convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and $r_s$ and $r_d$ are lengths. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.

charts.name: Static Spherical

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$

Radius at which the area of the spheres of the Einstein metric vanishes, $r_d = 2r_q^2/r_s$ with $r_q^2 = Q^2G/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4)$ the square of the charge radius, which is $Q^2/M$ in units with $G = c = 1$; $0 \le r_d \le r_s$, and $r_d = r_s$ is the extremal charge $Q^2 = 2M^2$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and take components of the Einstein metric in the chart $x^0 = ct$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$

Radius at which the area of the spheres of the Einstein metric vanishes, $r_d = 2r_q^2/r_s$ with $r_q^2 = Q^2G/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4)$ the square of the charge radius, which is $Q^2/M$ in units with $G = c = 1$; $0 \le r_d \le r_s$, and $r_d = r_s$ is the extremal charge $Q^2 = 2M^2$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \theta, \phi)$ on the Einstein metric, with the retarded time $u = ct - r_*$ a length, where $r_* = r + r_s\ln\left|r/r_s - 1\right|$.

charts.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$

Radius at which the area of the spheres of the Einstein metric vanishes, $r_d = 2r_q^2/r_s$ with $r_q^2 = Q^2G/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4)$ the square of the charge radius, which is $Q^2/M$ in units with $G = c = 1$; $0 \le r_d \le r_s$, and $r_d = r_s$ is the extremal charge $Q^2 = 2M^2$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi)$ on the Einstein metric, with the advanced time $v = ct + r_*$ a length, where $r_* = r + r_s\ln\left|r/r_s - 1\right|$.

charts.name: String Metric, Magnetic Charge

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$

Radius at which the area of the spheres of the Einstein metric vanishes, $r_d = 2r_q^2/r_s$ with $r_q^2 = Q^2G/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4)$ the square of the charge radius, which is $Q^2/M$ in units with $G = c = 1$; $0 \le r_d \le r_s$, and $r_d = r_s$ is the extremal charge $Q^2 = 2M^2$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius, and take components of the string metric $e^{2\varphi}g_{\mu\nu}$ of the magnetically charged hole, with $g_{\mu\nu}$ the Einstein metric and $e^{-2\varphi} = 1 - r_d/r$, in the chart $x^0 = ct$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: String Metric, Electric Charge

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$

Radius at which the area of the spheres of the Einstein metric vanishes, $r_d = 2r_q^2/r_s$ with $r_q^2 = Q^2G/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4)$ the square of the charge radius, which is $Q^2/M$ in units with $G = c = 1$; $0 \le r_d \le r_s$, and $r_d = r_s$ is the extremal charge $Q^2 = 2M^2$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and take components of the string metric $e^{2\varphi}g_{\mu\nu}$ of the electrically charged hole, with $g_{\mu\nu}$ the Einstein metric and $e^{2\varphi} = 1 - r_d/r$, in the chart $x^0 = ct$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

spacetimes.name: Einstein Static Universe
spacetimes.description: Albert Einstein's cosmology of 1917: dust spread uniformly through a round three sphere of fixed radius and held at rest by a positive cosmological constant. Minkowski, de Sitter, and anti-de Sitter space are each conformal to a region of it.
spacetimes.convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the one parameter is the radius $R$ of the three sphere, a length. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.

charts.name: Hyperspherical

parameters.description: Radius of the three sphere, a length; for dust of density $\rho$ the field equations with a cosmological constant $\Lambda$ fix $\Lambda = 1/R^2$ and $\rho = c^2/(4\pi GR^2)$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \chi, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\chi$, $\theta$, and $\phi$ angles on the three sphere. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Areal
domains: r = R \;\text{(the equator of } S^3\text{; the coordinates cover one hemisphere)}

parameters.description: Radius of the three sphere, a length; for dust of density $\rho$ the field equations with a cosmological constant $\Lambda$ fix $\Lambda = 1/R^2$ and $\rho = c^2/(4\pi GR^2)$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r = R\sin\chi$ the areal radius, which covers the hemisphere $\chi < \pi/2$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Einstein's Cartesian
domains: x^2 + y^2 + z^2 < R^2 \;\text{(one hemisphere of } S^3\text{)}

parameters.description: Radius of the three sphere, a length; for dust of density $\rho$ the field equations with a cosmological constant $\Lambda$ fix $\Lambda = 1/R^2$ and $\rho = c^2/(4\pi GR^2)$

charts.convention: We use Albert Einstein's coordinates of 1917, $(t, x, y, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $x$, $y$, and $z$ the lengths of the projection of the hemisphere $\chi < \pi/2$ onto its equatorial plane. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
charts.line_element: ds^2 = -c^2dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2 + \dfrac{\left(x\,dx + y\,dy + z\,dz\right)^2}{R^2 - x^2 - y^2 - z^2}

spacetimes.name: Einstein-Rosen Cylindrical Gravitational Waves
spacetimes.description: Exact vacuum solutions describing gravitational waves with cylindrical wave fronts and a single polarisation, converging on an axis, passing through it and spreading out again. Einstein's equations for them reduce to the flat cylindrical wave equation for one function and a quadrature for a second.
spacetimes.convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.

charts.name: Cylindrical

parameters.description: Wave amplitude, a dimensionless function of $t$ and $\rho$, with $e^{2\psi} = g_{zz}$; the spacetime is a vacuum exactly where it solves the flat cylindrical wave equation $\partial_\rho^2\psi + \partial_\rho\psi/\rho - \partial_t^2\psi = 0$ and $\gamma$ solves the two equations beside it; the pulse of Weber, Wheeler, and Bonnor, of width $a$ and amplitude $C$, is $\psi = \sqrt{2}\,C\sqrt{D_+ + a^2 + \rho^2 - c^2t^2}/D_+$ with $D_+^2 = (a^2 + \rho^2 - c^2t^2)^2 + 4a^2c^2t^2$

Dimensionless function of $t$ and $\rho$ fixed by $\psi$ through $\partial_\rho\gamma = \rho\left(\left(\partial_\rho\psi\right)^2 + \left(\partial_t\psi\right)^2\right)$ and $\partial_t\gamma = 2\rho\,\partial_\rho\psi\,\partial_t\psi$, and zero on a regular axis

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \rho, \phi, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, $\rho$ a length fixed by $g_{\phi\phi}\,g_{zz} = \rho^2$, and $z$ a length along the axis. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, so $\partial_t\psi = c^{-1}\partial\psi/\partial t$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Null

parameters.description: Wave amplitude, a dimensionless function of $u$ and $v$, with $e^{2\psi} = g_{zz}$; the spacetime is a vacuum exactly where it solves the flat cylindrical wave equation $2(v - u)\,\partial_u\partial_v\psi = \partial_v\psi - \partial_u\psi$ and $\gamma$ solves the two equations beside it

Dimensionless function of $u$ and $v$ fixed by $\psi$ through $\partial_u\gamma = -(v - u)\left(\partial_u\psi\right)^2$ and $\partial_v\gamma = (v - u)\left(\partial_v\psi\right)^2$, and zero on a regular axis

charts.convention: We use the retarded coordinate $u = ct - \rho$ and the advanced coordinate $v = ct + \rho$ of the cylindrical chart, both lengths, and $z$ a length along the axis. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
